title: Rheumatoid arthritis + intubation -> quadriparesis: atlantoaxial vertebral subluxation
vignette: A 56-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department due to several days of progressive dyspnea, productive cough, and fever. Today, her son found her very short of breath and obtunded. The patient has a history of hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, and long-standing rheumatoid arthritis. Examination reveals bilateral pneumonia and severe respiratory distress. The patient is lethargic without focal neurologic deficits. Urgent endotracheal intubation is performed for mechanical ventilation, and the patient is started on broad-spectrum antibiotics. Repeat examination 2 hours later shows that she has developed areflexic, flaccid paralysis of all extremities. Which of the following is the most likely cause of the neurologic deficits in this patient?

clues.note: Long-standing rheumatoid arthritis frequently involves the CERVICAL spine, especially the atlantoaxial (C1-C2) joint, causing instability/subluxation.
Neck EXTENSION during endotracheal intubation can acutely worsen atlantoaxial subluxation and compress the spinal cord.

clues.text: areflexic, flaccid paralysis of all extremities
clues.note: Acute quadriparesis that is flaccid and areflexic reflects acute spinal cord injury (spinal shock) - here from cervical cord compression.

whatMatters: Long-standing RA erodes the cervical spine (ATLANTOAXIAL SUBLUXATION). Neck extension during ENDOTRACHEAL INTUBATION acutely worsened the subluxation, COMPRESSING the cervical spinal cord -> acute quadriparesis (flaccid, areflexic = spinal shock). Answer E.
strategy: Link the timeline: RA (cervical instability) + intubation (neck manipulation) -> new quadriparesis = mechanical cord compression from vertebral subluxation. Reject cerebral septic emboli (would give focal/unilateral deficits, endocarditis stigmata), diabetic neuropathy (slowly progressive sensory, not acute quadriplegia), Guillain-Barre (ascending over days, not minutes post-intubation), and malignant hyperthermia (rigidity + hyperthermia after anesthetics, not flaccid paralysis).

eliminations.label: Cerebral septic emboli - focal, endocarditis stigmata
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: septic emboli to the brain (from endocarditis). ❌ WHY IT FAILS: emboli cause FOCAL/unilateral deficits, and there is no murmur or embolic stigmata; symmetric flaccid quadriparesis right after intubation fits cord compression. ✅ Correct if: infective endocarditis with focal neuro signs.

eliminations.label: Diabetic neuropathy - slow, sensory
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: chronic distal sensorimotor neuropathy from diabetes. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: it develops slowly (vibratory/proprioceptive loss), not acute quadriplegia minutes after intubation. ✅ Correct if: chronic stocking-glove sensory loss.

eliminations.label: Guillain-Barre - ascending over days
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: acute inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy with ascending flaccid weakness/areflexia. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: GBS evolves over DAYS to weeks (often post-infectious), not within 2 hours of intubation. ✅ Correct if: ascending weakness over days with albuminocytologic dissociation.

eliminations.label: Malignant hyperthermia - rigidity + hyperthermia
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: a hypermetabolic reaction to anesthetics (halothane, succinylcholine). ❌ WHY IT FAILS: it causes muscle RIGIDITY, hyperthermia, and myoglobinuria - not flaccid areflexic paralysis. ✅ Correct if: rising end-tidal CO2, rigidity, hyperthermia post-anesthesia.

reasoning: Neck extension during intubation acutely worsened the subluxation
Cervical spinal cord compression produced acute flaccid, areflexic quadriparesis (spinal shock)
mechanism: Long-standing RHEUMATOID ARTHRITIS causes chronic synovial inflammation that erodes joints, and it frequently involves the CERVICAL SPINE, producing vertebral malalignment (SUBLUXATION). The ATLANTOAXIAL joint (C1-C2) is most often affected because the atlas (C1) has a high degree of mobility relative to the axis (C2 odontoid), and pannus/ligament destruction (transverse ligament laxity) permits abnormal movement. Chronic subluxation may cause neck pain, stiffness, and myelopathic signs, but neck manipulation - such as EXTENSION during ENDOTRACHEAL INTUBATION - can ACUTELY worsen the subluxation and COMPRESS the cervical spinal cord (and/or vertebral arteries). Acute cord injury produces flaccid, AREFLEXIC paralysis below the lesion (SPINAL SHOCK), which later becomes spastic as spinal shock resolves - explaining this patient's sudden quadriparesis after intubation. Preoperative cervical imaging is considered in RA patients before airway manipulation. The distractors don't fit the abrupt, post-intubation, symmetric cord picture.

difficulty.label: 🧠 Knowledge
difficulty.text: First Aid Rheum/Neuro > RA cervical spine: atlantoaxial subluxation (C1-C2, odontoid); pannus/transverse ligament laxity; neck extension (intubation) -> acute cord compression -> quadriparesis; spinal shock = flaccid areflexic then spastic.

difficulty.label: 📖 Comprehension
difficulty.text: RA cervical subluxation + neck extension at intubation -> acute cord compression -> quadriparesis.

difficulty.label: 🔤 Vocab
difficulty.text: Unsure on atlantoaxial subluxation, spinal shock, pannus, or cervical myelopathy? Tell me which.

difficulty.label: 🨤 Distractor
difficulty.text: Septic emboli = focal; diabetic neuropathy = slow/sensory; GBS = days ascending; malignant hyperthermia = rigidity/fever.

difficulty.label: 🗒️ Other
difficulty.text: Bank: long-standing RA -> atlantoaxial subluxation; intubation neck extension -> acute cord compression (flaccid areflexic quadriparesis).

keywords.front: Trigger for acute cord compression in RA

keywords.back: Odontoid pannus + transverse ligament laxity -> instability
Cervical spine imaging before airway manipulation

firstAid.detail: Rheum: RA cervical instability; intubation -> cord compression.
Neuro > emboli, GBS, malignant hyperthermia, neuropathy.
Anesthesia > assess cervical spine before intubation.

memoryHook: Rheumatoid necks are loose at C1-C2; tip the head back to intubate and the wobbly joint pinches the cord - sudden flaccid quadriplegia.
